d: Step 2: sketch a box diagram, sanity-check it, and get the interviewer on board
goal: Your win today: sketch the news feed's two flows (publish and build) as boxes, decide how much API/schema detail to show, and check in with the interviewer before going deeper.
bookSections: Step 2: Propose high-level design and get buy-in, including the news feed publishing and feed-building high-level figures

stages.title: Treat Them Like a Teammate
stages.teaches: Step 2 budget: 10–15 minutes. Goal: an initial blueprint plus agreement from the interviewer. Collaborate: propose the plan, ask for feedback, treat the interviewer as a teammate; many good interviewers like to be involved. Draw box diagrams of the key components. Do rough maths to check the blueprint fits the scale constraints, thinking out loud, and ask whether the interviewer wants estimation before you do it. Walk through a few concrete use cases: it shapes the design and can surface edge cases you haven't thought of.
stages.interaction: Presentation-style chooser. Chat sim at minute 9. Three ways to start step 2, each played out as a short animated exchange after selection: (a) a 10-minute monologue building every detail (interviewer glazes, a 'signal' meter drops, and at minute 19 the interviewer reveals they wanted to focus elsewhere); (b) a 4-minute sketch of the main boxes, then 'Does this look like the right shape before I go deeper?' (interviewer nods and points at fan-out: meter rises) (correct); (c) asking the interviewer to draw the design for you (meter drops: collaboration isn't delegation). Learner can replay all three.
stages.check: Quiz: 'What does buy-in mean in step 2?' Options: The interviewer approves your salary / You and the interviewer agree the blueprint is a sensible base before you go deeper (correct) / You finish the whole design before asking anything / You let the interviewer choose every component.

stages.title: The Box Toolkit
stages.teaches: Typical boxes the book lists for the diagram: clients (mobile/web), APIs, web servers, data stores, cache, CDN, message queue. One line each: client = where requests start; load balancer = spreads traffic across web servers; web servers = handle requests (stateless so you can add more); data store = durable storage; cache = fast copy of hot data in memory; CDN = servers near users that serve static media like images and video; message queue = buffer that lets one part hand work to another asynchronously.
stages.interaction: Match-the-job. Left column: 7 box icons. Right column: 7 job descriptions in plain words, shuffled ('serves video from a server near the user', 'holds hot data in memory so we skip the DB', 'lets the post service hand slow work to workers later', etc.). Learner taps a box then a job to connect them; a correct pair draws a line and the box snaps into a mini whiteboard at the bottom. Wrong pair costs a heart and shows a hint.
stages.check: Quiz: 'Posts include video. Which box serves video quickly to users worldwide?' Options: Message queue / CDN (correct) / Load balancer / Relational database.

stages.title: Two Flows of a Feed
stages.teaches: The book splits the news feed at a high level into two flows. Feed publishing: when a user publishes a post, the post is written to cache and database, then pushed into friends' news feeds. Path: user (web/mobile) → load balancer → web servers → post service (stores the post in post cache + post DB), fanout service (pushes the post into friends' news feed cache), notification service (tells friends there's new content). News feed building: the feed is made by gathering friends' posts in reverse chronological order. Path: user → load balancer → web servers → news feed service → news feed cache (holds the post IDs that make up each feed). Splitting into flows is a reusable trick: most systems have a write path and a read path.
stages.interaction: Build-then-trace. (a) Two empty lanes labelled 'Publish a post' and 'Load my feed'. A palette of tiles (User, Load balancer, Web servers, Post service, Post cache, Post DB, Fanout service, News feed cache, Notification service, News feed service, plus 2 distractors: 'Search index', 'Payment service'). Learner taps tiles into each lane in path order; out-of-order or distractor taps shake. (b) Predict-then-watch: press 'Alice posts a photo' and first predict which box friends' feeds will read from later (Post DB / News feed cache (correct) / Notification service). Then animate a packet: through LB and web servers, splitting at the post service and fanout service, with 5 small packets flying to friends' feed-cache slots and a bell icon from the notification service. Then press 'Bob opens his feed' and the read packet goes LB → web servers → news feed service → news feed cache and returns a list of post IDs.
stages.check: Quiz: 'Which service puts a new post into friends' feeds?' Options: Notification service / Fanout service (correct) / Load balancer / News feed service.

stages.title: Pick the Zoom Level
stages.sub: API endpoints and schema: yes or no?
stages.teaches: Should step 2 include API endpoints and a database schema? The book says it depends on the problem. For a huge prompt like 'design Google search', that's too low-level for step 2. For a smaller one like a multiplayer poker game's backend, it's fair game. Talk to the interviewer about it. For the news feed, a couple of endpoints is a reasonable middle ground (Ch. 11 uses one to publish and one to retrieve the feed), with schema detail deferred.
stages.interaction: Zoom dial. Five prompt cards, each with a 3-position dial: 'Boxes only', 'Boxes + a few key APIs', 'Boxes + APIs + schema'. Learner sets the dial; the reveal explains. Answers: Design Google search → Boxes only; Multiplayer poker backend → Boxes + APIs + schema; News feed → Boxes + a few key APIs (e.g., publish post, get feed); URL shortener → Boxes + APIs + schema (small system, the API and the data model are the core); Design YouTube → Boxes only at first. Any answer that differs by one notch gets half credit plus the line 'when unsure, ask the interviewer'.
stages.check: Quiz: 'You're unsure whether to sketch the DB schema now. Best move?' Options: Always draw the full schema immediately / Never draw a schema in an interview / Ask the interviewer whether they'd like it now or later (correct) / Draw it secretly in the corner.

stages.title: Boss: Pushback at Minute 15
stages.teaches: Handling interviewer reactions in step 2 without stubbornness or over-engineering.
stages.interaction: Q.boss() with fixed choices: 'Adjust the blueprint', 'Defend with a reason', 'Park it for the deep dive', 'Ask a clarifying question'. Scenarios (answer, why): 1) 'Do we need a notification service at all?' → Defend with a reason (friends should hear about new posts; a short why, then move on). 2) 'Users mostly view on mobile with weak networks; video loads slowly.' → Adjust the blueprint (add CDN for media). 3) 'How exactly does fan-out handle a celebrity with millions of followers?' → Park it for the deep dive (acknowledge, note it, finish the blueprint first). 4) 'Make it faster.' → Ask a clarifying question (faster for posting or for loading the feed? which number?). 5) 'Your post service writes to the DB synchronously, then fans out synchronously. Posting feels slow.' → Adjust the blueprint (put fan-out behind a message queue so posting returns quickly). 6) 'Why a cache in front of the post DB?' → Defend with a reason (feeds are read far more than written; cache absorbs hot reads). Name: '🧱 The Whiteboard Wall'.
stages.check: Pass with at most 2 wrong; outro: 'Adjust when the point is valid, defend with a reason when it isn't, and park details until the deep dive.'

stages.title: Say It Like a Senior
stages.teaches: Narrating the diagram out loud, flow by flow.
stages.interaction: Q.drill(): prompt 'Scope is agreed. Walk the interviewer through your high-level news feed design.' Model answer (our words): 'I'll split it into two flows. Publishing: the client goes through a load balancer to stateless web servers. The post service saves the post to a database with a cache in front. A fanout service then pushes the post ID into each friend's feed in a news feed cache, and a notification service pings them. Reading: the client hits the news feed service, which reads the ready-made list of post IDs from the feed cache, newest first. Media goes to object storage and is served through a CDN. Before I go deeper, does this shape match what you want to focus on?'
stages.check: Self-grade checks: I split it into publish and read flows · I named the fanout service and the news feed cache · I mentioned load balancer and web servers · I ended by checking in with the interviewer.

caveats: The chapter's figures are deliberately high-level; how fan-out works (push on write vs pull on read, and the celebrity problem) is covered in Chapter 11. Here it's only previewed.
Object storage and CDN for video are our addition following the media requirement; the chapter's step 2 figures focus on the two flows.
Rough estimation in step 2 is optional; some interviewers skip it entirely, others insist. Ask first.
